title: Model Collapse Is Avoidable Even as Real Data Vanishes: A Sharp Criterion for Iterative Gaussian Estimation

paper.title: Model Collapse Is Avoidable Even as Real Data Vanishes: A Sharp Criterion for Iterative Gaussian Estimation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can cause a progressive degradation in model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse . Yet, currently, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theoretical research suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from model-generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a less restrictive and more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian data distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms,
and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2 2 -Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we then show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly.
However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times:
we show that the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero.
We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup,
and complement our theoretical work with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A growing body of empirical and theoretical work has raised the concern that machine learning generative models trained iteratively on data produced by earlier generations of themselves — rather than on real, independently sourced data — can drift away from the true underlying distribution over successive generations, a phenomenon often called model collapse ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ) . As more of the data on which models are trained is itself generated by other models, understanding the conditions under which this recursive process is destructive to the model and how we can deal with that has become an important theoretical question ( Bertrand et al., 2024 ; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Seddik et al., 2024 ; Dohmatob et al., 2025 ; Dohmatob et al., 2024 ; Barzilai and Shamir, 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Garg et al., 2026 ) . There are several approaches to iterative retraining, two of which are commonly referred to as Accumulate and Replace . In the Accumulate method, we start with a set of real data, and at each iteration, we augment the training set with newly generated data while retaining all data from previous iterations. In contrast, in the Replace method, the training set at each iteration consists only of the newly generated data from the previous iteration; all data from earlier iterations are discarded. The Accumulate method is generally considered a more realistic setting for iterative retraining and has been shown to exhibit degradation that remains bounded across iterations ( Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Seddik et al., 2024 ) . In contrast, the Replace method can lead to unbounded degradation, with the learned distribution progressively diverging from the original data distribution ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ) . Existing literature tries to theoretically explain the dramatic improvement of current top-tier generative models. This is done by considering the existence of independent real data in each iteration. However, it has only been investigated under the assumption that the real data can be perfectly separated from the generated data ( Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ; Garg et al., 2026 ) . In this case, an optimal weighting scheme for the separate real and generated data used for training has been studied ( He et al., 2026 ) . However, exact separation is not realistic ( Sadasivan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , and uncurated data is still commonly used. In this paper, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to bridge this gap by considering a less restrictive and more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. We study Accumulate -based iterative estimation of the mean 𝝁 ∈ ℝ d \boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and covariance matrix 𝚺 ∈ ℝ d × d \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} of a Gaussian data distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝁 , 𝚺 ) \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) , a standard setting in theoretical works on model collapse ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ) . At each round t t , a batch of new samples is drawn from a mixture of (i) the current fitted Gaussian model and (ii) the true distribution, and all data accumulated so far is used to refit the mean and covariance by standard empirical estimators, 𝝁 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)} and 𝚺 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{(t)} , but without distinguishing between real and generated samples. This setting strips away the complications of neural networks while retaining the essential recursive feedback loop and admits rigorous analysis. Our guiding question is: under what conditions does this process not collapse. In other words, when do the iterated estimators ( 𝝁 ( t ) , 𝚺 ( t ) ) (\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{(t)}) converge to the true ( 𝝁 , 𝚺 ) (\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) , and when do they instead settle on a biased, degenerate limit? We answer this question completely for both estimators. For the mean estimator, we also analyze the rate of convergence. Here, the mixing fraction α t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha_{t}\in[0,1] , the expected fraction of data in the new batch drawn from the current model, plays a decisive role, and we provide an explicit, checkable condition on how it may vary across rounds while still guaranteeing consistency. That separates collapse from non-collapse. Our main contributions include: • We prove that the mean estimator 𝝁 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)} is unbiased, while the covariance estimator 𝚺 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{(t)} is biased, with the exact bias given by − Cov ⁡ ( 𝝁 ( t ) ) -\Cov(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}) . • We provide a closed-form equivalent condition for the consistency of the estimated mean in L 2 L^{2} , the consistency of the covariance estimator in expected Frobenius norm, and the convergence to zero of the expected squared 2 2 -Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. • We use our result to show that several scenarios that naturally arise when scraping the web for data are sufficient to guarantee convergence, thereby preventing model collapse. First, convergence holds for an arbitrarily small but fixed positive fraction of real data ( 1 − α 1-\alpha ) at every iteration. Second, convergence still holds when the fraction of real data vanishes across iterations, provided that it does not vanish too quickly. • For a fixed synthetic fraction 0 ≤ α < 1 0\leq\alpha<1 (i.e., when not all data is generated), we derive the exact rate of convergence (up to constant factors) of the mean estimator to the true mean. Specifically, we prove that if less than half of each new batch is generated, then the rate of convergence matches the optimal rate. However, when more than half of each new batch is generated, the rate of convergence becomes arbitrarily slow as the fraction of synthetic data increases. This result motivates the ongoing research on the detection and curation of generated samples: it shows that for practical finite t t in the high-synthetic regime, synthetic data detection can substantially improve estimation accuracy. • We present an empirical investigation of the theoretical model that supports our theoretical results and provides further insight into the rate of convergence. • We complement our theoretical work with an empirical study of how different fixed real-data ratios affect the FID of a diffusion model iteratively trained on CIFAR-10, showing results that correlate with our theory.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Existing works have shown that under the Replace workflow, iterative retraining degrades without bound ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Dohmatob et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ) , whereas under the Accumulate workflow the degradation remains bounded ( Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Seddik et al., 2024 ) . Several works show that collapse can be avoided, but under restrictive conditions. Bertrand et al. (2024) prove the stability of iterative retraining on a mixture of real and synthetic data, but only locally, when the initial model is sufficiently close to the data distribution and the proportion of real data is sufficiently large. Barzilai and Shamir (2025) provide non-asymptotic guarantees under data accumulation; however, for a fixed sample size n n , their bound holds only up to a finite number of iterations t t that depends on n n , and thus does not cover the regime of fixed n n with t → ∞ t\to\infty . Moreover, beyond an initial (or fixed) real dataset, these works do not incorporate new real data at subsequent iterations. In practice, data scraped from the web at each iteration contains new real data alongside generated data. Several works study this setting ( Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ; Garg et al., 2026 ) , but either discard earlier data or assume that real and generated samples can be told apart, e.g., in order to weight them separately. The latter is unrealistic, since reliably detecting generated content remains an open problem ( Sadasivan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , although detection, when possible, can substantially mitigate collapse ( Drayson et al., 2025 ) . To the best of our knowledge, no prior work analyzes iterative retraining with accumulated data in which fresh real samples are not distinguished from generated ones.

sections.heading: 3 Theory
sections.text: In this section, we formalize the iterative retraining process, define the corresponding mean and covariance estimators, and state our main theoretical results, which characterize when the estimators converge to the true parameters and the rate at which this convergence occurs. Finally, we validate our results through experiments and provide additional insights into the rate of decay.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem setup: data generating process and estimators
sections.text: In the theoretical model, we consider the accumulate method, where the process is initialized with a dataset of real samples. Similar to a vast body of theoretical work on model collapse ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Dohmatob et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ; Dohmatob et al., 2025 ) , we assume that the real data distribution is a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, the training dataset is augmented with both generated and real data. Since the model does not know which samples are real and which are generated, it treats all samples identically and estimates the underlying distribution using the entire accumulated dataset. Formally, at each iteration, each newly added sample is drawn from the real distribution with some probability and from the current estimated distribution with the complementary probability. sections.heading: 3.2 Theoretical results
sections.text: In this section, we present our key theoretical results. In Section 3.2.1 , we establish that the mean estimator is unbiased and derive an explicit formula for the bias of the covariance estimator. In Section 3.2.2 , we provide an equivalent (if and only if) condition for the convergence of the estimated parameters to the truth, and hence for the convergence of the estimated distribution to the true distribution. We then show that the model converges when the fraction of real data is fixed and arbitrarily small, as well as when the fraction of real data tends to zero sufficiently slowly. In Section 3.2.3 , we analyze the convergence rate of the mean estimator. The proofs for all the claims are deferred to Appendix A .

Thus, any fixed positive fraction 1 − α 1-\alpha of real data in each batch suffices for consistency, even when the real samples added at each iteration are vastly outnumbered by the generated ones. sections.heading: 3.2.3 Rate of convergence
sections.text: We have shown that, for every fixed α < 1 \alpha<1 , the estimators are consistent. This result concerns the limit of infinitely many iterations. In practical training scenarios, however, only a finite number of iterations is performed. We, therefore, ask: how quickly do the estimated parameters converge to the true parameters? Below, we establish the rate of convergence for the mean estimator. In Section 3.3 , we show similar behavior for the covariance estimator. The next result gives the exact convergence rate and reveals a sharp transition at α = 1 2 \alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} . Theorem 3.6 (Rate of decay) . Assume the setup of Section 3.1 , α t ≡ α ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha_{t}\equiv\alpha\in[0,1] and n b ​ ( t ) ≡ n b n_{b}(t)\equiv n_{b} . At α = 1 2 \alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} a phase transition occurs, and for α > 1 2 \alpha>\tfrac{1}{2} the exponent 2 ​ ( 1 − α ) 2(1-\alpha) decreases linearly to 0 0 as α → 1 \alpha\to 1 . sections.heading: 4 Experiments with Diffusion Models
sections.text: Our paper focuses on theoretical contributions. Yet, to demonstrate that insights generalize beyond the theoretical setup, in Appendix D we present results of iterative training of a DDPM-based diffusion model ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , on the CIFAR-10 dataset ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) . We examine the effect of different fixed values of α \alpha , with no distinction between real and generated data, on the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) quality metric. Aligning with our theory: 1) for every α < 1 \alpha<1 , the FID improves upon its initial value at every iteration, although real and generated images are pooled indistinguishably; 2) for α = 1 \alpha=1 , the FID never improves but remains bounded; 3) the FID is ordered by α \alpha at every iteration, and its improvement slows as α \alpha grows; 4) for α = 0.25 < 1 2 \alpha=0.25<\tfrac{1}{2} , the curve follows that of α = 0 \alpha=0 up to a roughly constant offset, i.e., synthetic data inflates the constant but not the rate; and 5) discarding the generated images would improve the final FID far more for α = 0.75 > 1 2 \alpha=0.75>\tfrac{1}{2} than for α = 0.25 < 1 2 \alpha=0.25<\tfrac{1}{2} . An apparent gap between the theoretical setup and the diffusion experiments is that, for a large α < 1 \alpha<1 , the FID stops improving at some t t . This may result from the simple training strategy used (which could be improved) and the relatively simple diffusion model (which could be scaled up).

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Large generative models are commonly trained on data scraped from the web, an increasing share of which is generated by earlier models. Prior work shows that iterative training degrades performance: 1) without bound when earlier data is discarded, and 2) in a bounded manner when data accumulates. The continued improvement of generative models has been explained by the availability of fresh real data, but only under the unrealistic assumption that it can be perfectly separated from generated data. In this paper, we studied the more realistic setting in which fresh real and generated samples are pooled indistinguishably. We showed, for a tractable Gaussian data model, that the estimated distribution converges to the true one if and only if the share of fresh real information (quantified exactly) is not summable. Our results reveal that consistency holds for any fixed positive fraction of real data, and even for a fraction that vanishes slowly enough. Yet, the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as generated samples become more prevalent: it matches the rate of purely real data as long as generated samples are a minority of the newly collected data, and becomes arbitrarily slow once they are a majority. This motivates ongoing research on detecting and curating generated samples, and indicates when such efforts are worthwhile: as more data is collected, the gain from perfect detection is bounded when generated samples are a minority of the newly collected data, but grows without bound with the amount of collected data otherwise. Finally, while our work focuses on iterative training of generative models from a distribution estimation perspective, a compelling direction for future work is to explore whether even biased models can still generate augmented data that is useful for downstream tasks, similar to how low-level pre-processing can benefit downstream classification despite idealized information-theoretic principles ( Turgeman and Tirer, 2026 ) .

sections.text: Theorem 3.3 characterizes in closed form when this iterative estimation process converges to the true distribution. We now assemble it from Lemma A.10 and Theorems A.13 , A.22 , and A.24 . Proof. It suffices to show that (a) is equivalent to each of (b), (c), and (d). First, (a) ⇔ \Leftrightarrow (b) follows by combining Theorem A.13 with Lemma A.10 . Second, (a) ⇔ \Leftrightarrow (c) is exactly Theorem A.22 . sections.text: We first state a lemma that will be used in the following proof to compare sums and integrals. Lemma A.26 (Sum and integral equivalence) . Let a ∈ ℤ a\in\mathbb{Z} , let f : [ a , ∞ ) → ( 0 , ∞ ) f:[a,\infty)\to(0,\infty) be non-increasing, and fix h ≥ 0 h\geq 0 . Then for every integer b > a b>a : (a) ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≤ ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) ≤ f ⁡ ( a ) + ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x \displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\leq\sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)\leq f(a)+\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx ; in particular ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) = ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x + O ⁡ ( 1 ) \sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)=\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx+O(1) . (b) ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) ≍ ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x \displaystyle\sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)\asymp\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx . (c) ∫ a + h b + h f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≍ ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x \displaystyle\int_{a+h}^{b+h}f(x)\,dx\asymp\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx . All implied constants are independent of b b and depend only on f f and h h . If moreover ∫ a ∞ f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x = ∞ \int_{a}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=\infty , then the ratio of the two sides in (b) and (c) tends to 1 1 as b → ∞ b\to\infty , so ≍ \asymp may be replaced by ∼ \sim . Proof. Since f f is monotone on [ a , ∞ ) [a,\infty) , it is Riemann integrable on every compact sub-interval, so all integrals below are well defined and finite. Note also that f > 0 f>0 everywhere, so every quantity appearing in a denominator is nonzero. Throughout, we use the following elementary comparison: for every real y ≥ a y\geq a , monotonicity gives f ⁡ ( y ) ≥ f ⁡ ( x ) ≥ f ⁡ ( y + 1 ) f(y)\geq f(x)\geq f(y+1) for all x ∈ [ y , y + 1 ] x\in[y,y+1] , and hence f ⁡ ( y ) ≥ ∫ y y + 1 f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≥ f ⁡ ( y + 1 ) . f(y)\;\geq\;\int_{y}^{y+1}f(x)\,dx\;\geq\;f(y+1). (123) (a) Fix an integer b > a b>a . Applying the first inequality in ( 123 ) at y = t y=t and summing over t = a , … , b − 1 t=a,\dots,b-1 , ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) ≥ ∑ t = a b − 1 ∫ t t + 1 f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x = ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x , \sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)\;\geq\;\sum_{t=a}^{b-1}\int_{t}^{t+1}f(x)\,dx\;=\;\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx, which is the lower bound. For the upper bound, apply the second inequality in ( 123 ) at y = t − 1 y=t-1 , i.e. f ⁡ ( t ) ≤ ∫ t − 1 t f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x f(t)\leq\int_{t-1}^{t}f(x)\,dx , and sum over t = a + 1 , … , b − 1 t=a+1,\dots,b-1 (an empty sum if b = a + 1 b=a+1 ): ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) = f ⁡ ( a ) + ∑ t = a + 1 b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) ≤ f ⁡ ( a ) + ∑ t = a + 1 b − 1 ∫ t − 1 t f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x = f ⁡ ( a ) + ∫ a b − 1 f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≤ f ⁡ ( a ) + ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x , \sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)\;=\;f(a)+\sum_{t=a+1}^{b-1}f(t)\;\leq\;f(a)+\sum_{t=a+1}^{b-1}\int_{t-1}^{t}f(x)\,dx=f(a)+\int_{a}^{b-1}f(x)\,dx\;\leq\;f(a)+\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx, the last step because f > 0 f>0 . Consequently, writing D ⁡ ( b ) ≔ ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) − ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x D(b)\coloneqq\sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)-\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx , we have shown 0 ≤ D ⁡ ( b ) ≤ f ⁡ ( a ) for every integer ​ b > a , 0\;\leq\;D(b)\;\leq\;f(a)\qquad\text{for every integer }b>a, (124) which is precisely the assertion ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) = ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x + O ⁡ ( 1 ) \sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)=\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx+O(1) , with implied constant f ⁡ ( a ) f(a) independent of b b . (b) Fix an integer b > a b>a ; then b ≥ a + 1 b\geq a+1 , so by ( 123 ) applied at y = a y=a , ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≥ ∫ a a + 1 f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≥ f ⁡ ( a + 1 ) > 0 ⇒ 1 f ⁡ ( a + 1 ) ​ ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≥ 1 . \int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\;\geq\;\int_{a}^{a+1}f(x)\,dx\;\geq\;f(a+1)\;>\;0\Rightarrow\frac{1}{f(a+1)}\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\geq 1. (125) Combining ( 124 ) and ( 125 ), ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) ≤ f ⁡ ( a ) + ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≤ f ⁡ ( a ) f ⁡ ( a + 1 ) ​ ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x + ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x , \sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)\;\leq\;f(a)+\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\;\leq\;\frac{f(a)}{f(a+1)}\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx+\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx, so that, together with the lower bound from (a), ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≤ ∑ t = a b − 1 f ⁡ ( t ) ≤ ( 1 + f ⁡ ( a ) f ⁡ ( a + 1 ) ) ​ ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x . \int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\;\leq\;\sum_{t=a}^{b-1}f(t)\;\leq\;\Big(1+\tfrac{f(a)}{f(a+1)}\Big)\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx. Both constants are independent of b b , proving (b). (c) Fix h ≥ 0 h\geq 0 and an integer b > a b>a . The change of variables x = y + h x=y+h gives ∫ a + h b + h f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x = ∫ a b f ⁡ ( y + h ) ​ 𝑑 y \int_{a+h}^{b+h}f(x)\,dx=\int_{a}^{b}f(y+h)\,dy , and since f ⁡ ( y + h ) ≤ f ⁡ ( y ) f(y+h)\leq f(y) for h ≥ 0 h\geq 0 , ∫ a + h b + h f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x ≤ ∫ a b f ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x . \int_{a+h}^{b+h}f(x)\,dx\;\leq\;\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx. sections.heading: Appendix B The value of identifying real samples
sections.text: We quantify the gain from perfect detection of synthetic samples under the setting of Theorem 3.6 , i.e., α t ≡ α \alpha_{t}\equiv\alpha and n b ​ ( t ) ≡ n b n_{b}(t)\equiv n_{b} . The pool contains, in expectation, N oracle ≔ ( 1 − α ) ​ N t + α ​ n r N_{\mathrm{oracle}}\coloneqq(1-\alpha)N_{t}+\alpha n_{r} real samples, which is approximately the sample size available to an oracle that identifies and keeps only them. On the other hand, the sample mean of N N i.i.d. real samples has an error of Tr ⁡ ( 𝚺 ) / N \Tr(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})/N , so the pooled estimator has the effective sample size N eff ≔ Tr ⁡ ( 𝚺 ) / 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝝁 ( t ) − 𝝁 ‖ 2 2 ] = Tr ⁡ ( 𝚺 ) / Tr ⁡ ( 𝑪 t ) N_{\mathrm{eff}}\coloneqq\Tr(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})/\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\Tr(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})/\Tr(\boldsymbol{C}_{t}) (by ( 11 )), i.e., the number of i.i.d. real samples that attain the same error. The gain from perfect detection is the ratio G α ​ ( N t ) ≔ N oracle N eff = ( ( 1 − α ) ​ N t + α ​ n r ) ​ Tr ⁡ ( 𝑪 t ) Tr ⁡ ( 𝚺 ) . G_{\alpha}(N_{t})\coloneqq\frac{N_{\mathrm{oracle}}}{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}=\bigl((1-\alpha)N_{t}+\alpha n_{r}\bigr)\,\frac{\Tr(\boldsymbol{C}_{t})}{\Tr(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}. (150) As N t → ∞ N_{t}\to\infty , Theorem 3.6 gives G α ​ ( N t ) ≍ { 1 , 0 ≤ α < 1 2 , ln ⁡ N t , α = 1 2 , N t 2 ​ α − 1 , 1 2 < α < 1 . G_{\alpha}(N_{t})\asymp\begin{cases}1,&0\leq\alpha<\tfrac{1}{2},\\ \ln N_{t},&\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2},\\ N_{t}^{2\alpha-1},&\tfrac{1}{2}<\alpha<1.\end{cases} (151) In words, when generated samples are a minority of each new batch, perfect detection improves the effective sample size by at most a constant factor, no matter how much data is collected. When they are a majority, the improvement grows without bound as more data is collected. Moreover, the gain grows with α \alpha in the long run: for any 0 ≤ α < α ′ < 1 0\leq\alpha<\alpha^{\prime}<1 with α ′ > 1 2 \alpha^{\prime}>\tfrac{1}{2} , we have G α ′ ​ ( N t ) / G α ​ ( N t ) → ∞ G_{\alpha^{\prime}}(N_{t})/G_{\alpha}(N_{t})\to\infty as N t → ∞ N_{t}\to\infty . Thus, asymptotically, the gain from detection is largest exactly where the pooled estimator converges most slowly. At a fixed, finite N t N_{t} , however, the gain does not increase all the way to α = 1 \alpha=1 . At the two extremes, G 0 ​ ( N t ) = 1 , 1 ≤ G 1 ​ ( N t ) = n r ​ Tr ⁡ ( 𝑪 t ) Tr ⁡ ( 𝚺 ) ≤ 2 , G_{0}(N_{t})=1,\qquad 1\leq G_{1}(N_{t})=n_{r}\,\frac{\Tr(\boldsymbol{C}_{t})}{\Tr(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}\leq 2, (152) where the bounds follow from Proposition 3.5 and Lemma 3.2 . At α = 0 \alpha=0 there is nothing to detect, and at α = 1 \alpha=1 the oracle retains only the n r n_{r} initial real samples. For fixed t t , G α ​ ( N t ) G_{\alpha}(N_{t}) is continuous in α \alpha , and by ( 151 ), for any fixed α ∈ ( 1 2 , 1 ) \alpha\in(\tfrac{1}{2},1) it exceeds 2 2 once N t N_{t} is large enough. Hence, for large but finite N t N_{t} , the gain is maximized at some α \alpha strictly between 0 0 and 1 1 . In practice, detection is therefore worth most when generated data dominates, but real data is still being added in meaningful amounts. The potential for such detection to improve performance is supported empirically by prior work on identifying and curating model-generated data ( Drayson et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Appendix D Experiments with Diffusion Models
sections.text: While our paper focuses on theoretical contributions, in this section we empirically examine the extent to which the behavior observed in a practical deep learning setting is consistent with our theoretical results.

sections.heading: Data and protocol.
sections.text: We consider CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) and a diffusion model ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song et al., 2021b ) based on the DDPM framework ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , using the U-Net implementation of Zou () ( https://github.com/zoubohao/DenoisingDiffusionProbabilityModel-ddpm- ), and train unconditional models. We split the 50,000 50{,}000 CIFAR-10 training images into a class-balanced validation set of 5,000 5{,}000 images and 45,000 45{,}000 images available for training; the 10,000 10{,}000 test images are used only for evaluation. We set n r = n b = 5,000 n_{r}=n_{b}=5{,}000 and t max = 9 t_{\max}=9 , so that the pool at iteration t t contains N t = n r + ( t − 1 ) ​ n b N_{t}=n_{r}+(t-1)n_{b} images and the final pool, N 9 = 45,000 N_{9}=45{,}000 , uses all available training images. We consider four fixed mixing fractions, α ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.75 , 1 } \alpha\in\{0,0.25,0.75,1\} . At t = 1 t=1 we train a DDPM on n r n_{r} class-balanced real images; this model is shared by all four values of α \alpha . At each iteration t ≥ 2 t\geq 2 , we accumulate the previous pool with α ​ n b \alpha n_{b} samples generated by the model of iteration t − 1 t-1 and ( 1 − α ) ​ n b (1-\alpha)n_{b} previously unused, class-balanced real images, and the training treats real and generated images identically: minibatches are drawn uniformly from the pool, with no labels, reweighting or filtering. Unlike the theoretical setup, where each sample is drawn from the mixture independently, here the numbers of generated and real images in each batch are fixed. This keeps the consumption of real images exact and class-balanced, and differs negligibly from independent draws, whose count of generated images fluctuates by less than 1 % 1\% of the batch (one standard deviation) for n b = 5,000 n_{b}=5{,}000 .

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: All models share one recipe: 1,000 1{,}000 diffusion steps with a linear noise schedule from 10 − 4 10^{-4} to 0.02 0.02 , the ϵ \epsilon -prediction objective, Adam with learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} after a 5,000 5{,}000 -step linear warm-up, batch size 128 128 , gradient clipping at 1 1 , dropout 0.1 0.1 , and an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights with decay 0.9999 0.9999 . All sampling uses the EMA weights and DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) with 200 200 steps. We fix the number of optimization steps rather than the number of epochs, so that pool size is not confounded with the amount of computation. In each iteration t t the training is from scratch on the whole pool, except for α = 0.75 \alpha=0.75 and t ≥ 4 t\geq 4 , where we use warm-start from the previous iteration’s model with learning rate of lower order.

sections.heading: Checkpoint selection.
sections.text: Since diffusion models overfit on datasets of this size, each model should be trained neither too little nor too long, so that pools of different sizes are compared fairly. We save a checkpoint every 50,000 50{,}000 steps and select the one minimizing the FID between 10,000 10{,}000 generated samples and the validation set; we report the FID of the same samples against the test set, which is never used for selection. The default budget is 200,000 200{,}000 steps; iterations in which the validation FID was still decreasing at the end of the budget were retrained with a larger budget (up to 800,000 800{,}000 steps), which was needed only for α ∈ { 0 , 0.25 } \alpha\in\{0,0.25\} . Validation and test FIDs selected the same checkpoint in every iteration, and over all checkpoints they differed by a nearly constant offset of 2.44 ± 0.07 2.44\pm 0.07 .

sections.heading: FID values.
sections.text: We compute FID with clean-fid ( Parmar et al., 2022 ) from 10,000 10{,}000 DDIM samples against the held-out test set. Published DDPM results on CIFAR-10 (e.g., 3.17 3.17 in Ho et al. (2020) ) use 50,000 50{,}000 samples, 1,000 1{,}000 -step sampling and training-set statistics, which yields substantially lower values: for our best model ( α = 0 \alpha=0 , t = 9 t=9 , trained on 45,000 45{,}000 images), 50,000 50{,}000 samples against the training set give 5.1 5.1 , compared with 9.7 9.7 on the test set. Our FIDs are therefore comparable across the curves of Figure 6 , but not to published numbers.

sections.heading: Reporting.
sections.text: We report the test FID of the selected checkpoint as a function of N t N_{t} for each α \alpha , for a single training seed. The horizontal line is the α = 0 \alpha=0 model at t = 9 t=9 , i.e., a DDPM trained on all 45,000 45{,}000 training images with the same protocol. From duplicate runs, differences below ≈ 0.5 \approx 0.5 FID between consecutive iterations are within run-to-run variation. We expect the curves for α < 1 \alpha<1 to approach this reference value, whereas for α = 1 \alpha=1 , where no new real data are introduced, we expect the FID to approach a finite limiting value. All experiments were run on a server with eight NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, training one model per GPU. Training costs about 3.9 3.9 GPU-hours per 100,000 100{,}000 steps including checkpoint evaluation, e.g., about 8 8 , 15 15 and 31 31 hours for budgets of 200,000 200{,}000 , 400,000 400{,}000 and 800,000 800{,}000 steps; the runs shown in Figure 6 total roughly 400 400 GPU-hours. Figure 6: Test FID of DDPM on CIFAR-10 as a function of the pool size N t N_{t} , for mixing fractions α ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.75 , 1 } \alpha\in\{0,0.25,0.75,1\} (single seed). At each iteration, the checkpoint with the lowest validation FID is selected and its test FID is reported. The dashed line is the α = 0 \alpha=0 model at t = 9 t=9 , trained on all 45,000 45{,}000 training images (FID 9.7 9.7 on the test set, and 5.1 5.1 with 50,000 50{,}000 samples against the training set; see text). Differences below ≈ 0.5 \approx 0.5 FID between consecutive iterations are within run-to-run variation.

sections.heading: Comparison with the theory.
sections.text: The central prediction of our theory holds: although real and generated images are pooled and treated identically, with no detection, labeling or reweighting, every α < 1 \alpha<1 improves on the initial model, whereas α = 1 \alpha=1 degrades. At every iteration t ≥ 2 t\geq 2 , the FID for α ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.75 } \alpha\in\{0,0.25,0.75\} is below its initial value of 33.8 33.8 , while for α = 1 \alpha=1 it never falls below it. Thus, a fixed fraction of fresh real data suffices to avoid collapse even when it cannot be told apart from generated data. This comparison is meaningful beyond the Gaussian setting because FID is the squared 2-Wasserstein distance between Gaussians fitted to the Inception features of generated and test images, i.e., the quantity of Theorem 3.3 evaluated in a feature space. The finer predictions carry over as well. First, the curves are ordered by α \alpha at every iteration t ≥ 2 t\geq 2 : a larger fraction of generated data always yields a worse model. Second, the improvement slows as α \alpha grows, in line with Theorem 3.6 : from N 1 = 5,000 N_{1}=5{,}000 to N 3 = 15,000 N_{3}=15{,}000 , the FID decreases by 19.9 19.9 for α = 0 \alpha=0 , 16.7 16.7 for α = 0.25 \alpha=0.25 and only 6.8 6.8 for α = 0.75 \alpha=0.75 , the one value above 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} , whose predicted rate N t − 1 / 2 N_{t}^{-1/2} is slower than the rate N t − 1 N_{t}^{-1} of α < 1 2 \alpha<\tfrac{1}{2} . For α = 0.25 \alpha=0.25 , the curve follows that of α = 0 \alpha=0 with a roughly constant offset of 3 3 – 4 4 FID, consistent with synthetic data inflating the constant but not the exponent. Third, at α = 1 \alpha=1 the FID rises from 33.8 33.8 to 39.7 39.7 , with increments that shrink over the last iterations, matching the bounded, non-decreasing error of Propositions 3.5 and A.27 . The value of identifying real samples (Section 3.2.3 ) is also visible. Discarding all generated images would leave, at t = 9 t=9 , 35,000 35{,}000 real images for α = 0.25 \alpha=0.25 and 15,000 15{,}000 for α = 0.75 \alpha=0.75 , i.e., the α = 0 \alpha=0 model at N t = 35,000 N_{t}=35{,}000 (FID 10.3 10.3 ) and at N t = 15,000 N_{t}=15{,}000 (FID 13.8 13.8 ). Compared with FIDs of 13.5 13.5 and above 27 27 , respectively, perfect detection would gain about 3 3 FID for α = 0.25 < 1 2 \alpha=0.25<\tfrac{1}{2} , but more than 13 13 for α = 0.75 > 1 2 \alpha=0.75>\tfrac{1}{2} , as the theory predicts.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.00259v1 [stat.ML] 30 Oct 2026 Model Collapse Is Avoidable Even as Real Data Vanishes: A Sharp Criterion for Iterative Gaussian Estimation Roy Turgeman Affiliation: Faculty of Engineering Affiliation: Bar-Ilan University Affiliation: Ramat Gan, Israel Tom Tirer Affiliation: Faculty of Engineering Affiliation: Bar-Ilan University Affiliation: Ramat Gan, Israel Abstract Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can cause a progressive degradation in model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse . Yet, currently, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theoretical research suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from model-generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a less restrictive and more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian data distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms, and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2 2 -Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we then show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly. However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times: we show that the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup, and complement our theoretical work with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory . 1 Introduction A growing body of empirical and theoretical work has raised the concern that machine learning generative models trained iteratively on data produced by earlier generations of themselves — rather than on real, independently sourced data — can drift away from the true underlying distribution over successive generations, a phenomenon often called model collapse ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ) . As more of the data on which models are trained is itself generated by other models, understanding the conditions under which this recursive process is destructive to the model and how we can deal with that has become an important theoretical question ( Bertrand et al., 2024 ; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Seddik et al., 2024 ; Dohmatob et al., 2025 ; Dohmatob et al., 2024 ; Barzilai and Shamir, 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Garg et al., 2026 ) . There are several approaches to iterative retraining, two of which are commonly referred to as Accumulate and Replace . In the Accumulate method, we start with a set of real data, and at each iteration, we augment the training set with newly generated data while retaining all data from previous iterations. In contrast, in the Replace method, the training set at each iteration consists only of the newly generated data from the previous iteration; all data from earlier iterations are discarded. The Accumulate method is generally considered a more realistic setting for iterative retraining and has been shown to exhibit degradation that remains bounded across iterations ( Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Seddik et al., 2024 ) . In contrast, the Replace method can lead to unbounded degradation, with the learned distribution progressively diverging from the original data distribution ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ) . Existing literature tries to theoretically explain the dramatic improvement of current top-tier generative models. This is done by considering the existence of independent real data in each iteration. However, it has only been investigated under the assumption that the real data can be perfectly separated from the generated data ( Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ; Garg et al., 2026 ) . In this case, an optimal weighting scheme for the separate real and generated data used for training has been studied ( He et al., 2026 ) . However, exact separation is not realistic ( Sadasivan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , and uncurated data is still commonly used. In this paper, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to bridge this gap by considering a less restrictive and more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. We study Accumulate -based iterative estimation of the mean 𝝁 ∈ ℝ d \boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and covariance matrix 𝚺 ∈ ℝ d × d \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} of a Gaussian data distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝁 , 𝚺 ) \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) , a standard setting in theoretical works on model collapse ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ) . At each round t t , a batch of new samples is drawn from a mixture of (i) the current fitted Gaussian model and (ii) the true distribution, and all data accumulated so far is used to refit the mean and covariance by standard empirical estimators, 𝝁 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)} and 𝚺 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{(t)} , but without distinguishing between real and generated samples. This setting strips away the complications of neural networks while retaining the essential recursive feedback loop and admits rigorous analysis. Our guiding question is: under what conditions does this process not collapse. In other words, when do the iterated estimators ( 𝝁 ( t ) , 𝚺 ( t ) ) (\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{(t)}) converge to the true ( 𝝁 , 𝚺 ) (\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) , and when do they instead settle on a biased, degenerate limit? We answer this question completely for both estimators. For the mean estimator, we also analyze the rate of convergence. Here, the mixing fraction α t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha_{t}\in[0,1] , the expected fraction of data in the new batch drawn from the current model, plays a decisive role, and we provide an explicit, checkable condition on how it may vary across rounds while still guaranteeing consistency. That separates collapse from non-collapse. Our main contributions include: • We prove that the mean estimator 𝝁 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)} is unbiased, while the covariance estimator 𝚺 ( t ) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{(t)} is biased, with the exact bias given by − Cov ⁡ ( 𝝁 ( t ) ) -\Cov(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}) . • We provide a closed-form equivalent condition for the consistency of the estimated mean in L 2 L^{2} , the consistency of the covariance estimator in expected Frobenius norm, and the convergence to zero of the expected squared 2 2 -Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. • We use our result to show that several scenarios that naturally arise when scraping the web for data are sufficient to guarantee convergence, thereby preventing model collapse. First, convergence holds for an arbitrarily small but fixed positive fraction of real data ( 1 − α 1-\alpha ) at every iteration. Second, convergence still holds when the fraction of real data vanishes across iterations, provided that it does not vanish too quickly. • For a fixed synthetic fraction 0 ≤ α < 1 0\leq\alpha<1 (i.e., when not all data is generated), we derive the exact rate of convergence (up to constant factors) of the mean estimator to the true mean. Specifically, we prove that if less than half of each new batch is generated, then the rate of convergence matches the optimal rate. However, when more than half of each new batch is generated, the rate of convergence becomes arbitrarily slow as the fraction of synthetic data increases. This result motivates the ongoing research on the detection and curation of generated samples: it shows that for practical finite t t in the high-synthetic regime, synthetic data detection can substantially improve estimation accuracy. • We present an empirical investigation of the theoretical model that supports our theoretical results and provides further insight into the rate of convergence. • We complement our theoretical work with an empirical study of how different fixed real-data ratios affect the FID of a diffusion model iteratively trained on CIFAR-10, showing results that correlate with our theory. 2 Related work Existing works have shown that under the Replace workflow, iterative retraining degrades without bound ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Dohmatob et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ) , whereas under the Accumulate workflow the degradation remains bounded ( Gerstgrasser et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Seddik et al., 2024 ) . Several works show that collapse can be avoided, but under restrictive conditions. Bertrand et al. (2024) prove the stability of iterative retraining on a mixture of real and synthetic data, but only locally, when the initial model is sufficiently close to the data distribution and the proportion of real data is sufficiently large. Barzilai and Shamir (2025) provide non-asymptotic guarantees under data accumulation; however, for a fixed sample size n n , their bound holds only up to a finite number of iterations t t that depends on n n , and thus does not cover the regime of fixed n n with t → ∞ t\to\infty . Moreover, beyond an initial (or fixed) real dataset, these works do not incorporate new real data at subsequent iterations. In practice, data scraped from the web at each iteration contains new real data alongside generated data. Several works study this setting ( Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ; Garg et al., 2026 ) , but either discard earlier data or assume that real and generated samples can be told apart, e.g., in order to weight them separately. The latter is unrealistic, since reliably detecting generated content remains an open problem ( Sadasivan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , although detection, when possible, can substantially mitigate collapse ( Drayson et al., 2025 ) . To the best of our knowledge, no prior work analyzes iterative retraining with accumulated data in which fresh real samples are not distinguished from generated ones. 3 Theory In this section, we formalize the iterative retraining process, define the corresponding mean and covariance estimators, and state our main theoretical results, which characterize when the estimators converge to the true parameters and the rate at which this convergence occurs. Finally, we validate our results through experiments and provide additional insights into the rate of decay. 3.1 Problem setup: data generating process and estimators In the theoretical model, we consider the accumulate method, where the process is initialized with a dataset of real samples. Similar to a vast body of theoretical work on model collapse ( Shumailov et al., 2024 ; Alemohammad et al., 2024 ; Kazdan et al., 2025 ; Dohmatob et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2026 ; Dohmatob et al., 2025 ) , we assume that the real data distribution is a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, the training dataset is augmented with both generated and real data. Since the model does not know which samples are real and which are generated, it treats all samples identically and estimates the underlying distribution using the entire accumulated dataset. Formally, at each iteration, each newly added sample is drawn from the real distribution with some probability and from the current estimated distribution with the complementary probability. In Section 3.2.1 , we establish that the mean estimator is unbiased and derive an explicit formula for the bias of the covariance estimator. In Section 3.2.2 , we provide an equivalent (if and only if) condition for the convergence of the estimated parameters to the truth, and hence for the convergence of the estimated distribution to the true distribution. We then show that the model converges when the fraction of real data is fixed and arbitrarily small, as well as when the fraction of real data tends to zero sufficiently slowly.
